title: A rational torus point separates finitely many distinct algebraic characters
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], let $r\geq0$ be an integer, and let $T$ be a $k$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] isomorphic to $(\mathbf G_{m,k})^r$, where $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$ [def-sc-gm-ga] for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$. A character of $T$ means a homomorphism of $k$-group schemes $\chi:T\to\mathbf G_{m,k}$. For every finite set $\Omega$ of pairwise distinct characters of $T$, there exists $s\in T(k)$ such that $\chi_k(s)\ne\psi_k(s)$ whenever $\chi,\psi\in\Omega$ and $\chi\ne\psi$. Equivalently, evaluation at $s$ is injective on $\Omega$. The assertion includes $r=0$ and $\Omega=\varnothing$, and imposes no characteristic restriction.

source.place: Lemma 16.42, proof, printed p.339: the proper closed character-equality loci S_ij and the choice of s outside their finite union; character and split-torus conventions in Theorem 12.9 and Definition 12.14, printed pp.233--236.

proof.text: Fix an isomorphism $\iota:(\mathbf G_m)^r\xrightarrow{\sim}T$. By [lem-sfb-split-torus-hom-matrices] with target rank $1$, each $\chi\circ\iota$ has a unique exponent vector $n_\chi\in\mathbf Z^r$, with value $\prod_a t_a^{n_{\chi,a}}$ on every algebra. Distinct characters have distinct vectors, since composition with an isomorphism is injective. If $r=0$, there is only the empty vector, hence at most one character; the identity point suffices. Henceforth $r>0$.

source.place: Theorem 12.9(a), printed pp.233–234; Lemma 16.42, proof, printed p.339 (distinct weights).

proof.text: The field $k$ is infinite: otherwise the nonconstant polynomial $\prod_{a\in k}(X-a)-1$ would have no root, contradicting algebraic closedness [def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Work in $R=k[X_1,\ldots,X_r]$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring]. For each ordered pair $(\chi,\psi)\in\Omega^2$ with $\chi\ne\psi$, put $c_a=\max(0,-n_{\chi,a},-n_{\psi,a})$ and $P_{\chi\psi}=X^{c+n_\chi}-X^{c+n_\psi}$. The exponents are nonnegative and distinct, so the coefficient at $c+n_\chi$ is $1$; thus $P_{\chi\psi}\ne0$ in every characteristic.

source.place: Lemma 16.42, proof, printed p.339: explicit polynomial equations for the character-equality loci; elementary coordinate expansion.

proof.text: By [lem-weil-pbc-polynomial-ring-domain], $R$ is an integral domain. Therefore the finite product $Q=(\prod_{a=1}^r X_a)\prod_{\chi\ne\psi}P_{\chi\psi}$ is nonzero: each variable is nonzero by its coefficient $1$, every pair factor was proved nonzero, and induction on the finite family uses the absence of zero divisors. An empty pair product is $1$.

source.place: Lemma 16.42, proof, printed p.339: finite union of proper character-equality loci; coordinate product argument.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-mvpolynomial-infinite-evaluation] to $Q$ and $0$ over the infinite domain $k$. If $Q(t)=0$ for every $t\in k^r$, that statement gives $Q=0$, a contradiction. Thus choose $t$ with $Q(t)\ne0$. Since evaluation is a ring homomorphism [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring], every $t_a$ and every $P_{\chi\psi}(t)$ is nonzero.

source.place: Lemma 16.42, proof, printed p.339: choice of a rational point outside the finite union, expanded using polynomial evaluation.

proof.text: The nonzero coordinates give $t\in(\mathbf G_m)^r(k)$; set $s=\iota_k(t)$. For each distinct pair, $P_{\chi\psi}(t)=(\prod_a t_a^{c_a})(\chi_k(s)-\psi_k(s))$. The first factor is a unit, so $P_{\chi\psi}(t)\ne0$ implies $\chi_k(s)\ne\psi_k(s)$. This proves injectivity on $\Omega$; when $\Omega$ is empty or a singleton the pairwise conclusion is vacuous and the identity point also works.

source.place: Lemma 16.42, proof, printed p.339: the chosen point separates all distinct weights; explicit cancellation of the denominator-clearing monomial.

proof_origin.place: Lemma 16.42, proof, printed p.339; Theorem 12.9(a), printed pp.233–234. Agent-written coordinate expansion of the finite closed-locus avoidance sentence.
